transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

They sent me here. I was at the station, and... well, I kept moving the airway bags into a pattern. I knew it was right. I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud while I was doing it, and my lieutenant came over and told me to stop. 

But I wouldn't step away. I couldn't. It felt like the whole bay would just go bad if I broke the sequence. So they told me I had to come see you.
Did you feel like you had to arrange the airway bags in that specific pattern?

Yeah, exactly. Like I was just saying, I really had to do it. It wasn't a choice. I had to put them in that exact pattern and... keep saying the dispatch numbers out loud. When my lieutenant told me to stop, I just couldn't step away. I knew if I broke that sequence, the whole bay was going to go bad. So, yes, I had to.
Do you ever feel the need to repeat certain behaviors or rituals when you're not at the fire station?
No, not really. It's... it's just at the station. I mean, I don't do anything like that at home or anywhere else. It's just when I'm there, with the gear.
Do you have thoughts that keep repeating in your mind, even when you're not at the fire station?

No, I don't think so. It's... my mind is pretty clear when I'm away from work. I don't have thoughts getting stuck on a loop or anything like that. It's really just that feeling I get about the gear when I'm at the station.
Did you feel anxious or uncomfortable when your lieutenant told you to stop arranging the airway bags?

Yeah, I did. I felt really anxious. When he told me to stop, it was like... like this sudden panic hit me. I knew that if I didn't finish the pattern, something terrible was going to happen right there in the bay. So, yeah, it made me very uncomfortable to even think about stopping.
Do you consider yourself a perfectionist?

No, I don't think so. I wouldn't call myself a perfectionist. I mean, I don't need everything in my life to be spotless or perfectly organized or anything like that. It's really just... it's just that specific thing with the gear at work. Outside of that, I'm pretty laid back about how things are.
Have you ever had any other behaviors or habits that you felt compelled to do, even if they didn't make sense to you or others?

No, not really. I mean... I don't have any other habits like that. It's really just the airway bags at the station. I don't have anything else I feel like I have to do, or any other routines I'm stuck on. Just that one thing.
Did you honestly believe that something terrible was going to happen if you didn't finish the pattern with the airway bags?

Yeah, I really did. I mean, that's the whole reason they sent me here. At the station, I just kept moving the airway bags into this pattern that I knew was right, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud while I did it. When my lieutenant told me to stop, I wouldn't step away. I just couldn't. It felt like... like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. So, yes, I honestly believed it.
Did you think that not finishing the pattern would actually cause something bad to happen, like a real event?

I didn't really have a specific picture in my head of what it would be. Like, I didn't think there was going to be an ambulance crash or a fire or something like that. It wasn't a specific event I could name. 

It was just... this overwhelming feeling that things would go bad. The whole bay would just be wrong, or tainted somehow. I don't really know how else to describe it, I just didn't know exactly what would happen. I just knew I couldn't stop or else it would.
Did you think that not finishing the pattern would actually cause something bad to happen in a way that was outside of your control or unrelated to your actions at the station?

No, not really. I didn't think about it like... like it was going to cause some random disaster somewhere else or something totally outside of my control. It was just right there in front of me. 

It felt completely tied to what I was doing with the bags at that exact moment. Like I said, I just felt like the bay itself would be wrong or ruined if I didn't finish it. I didn't really think about it connecting to anything else outside of that.
Did you think that your belief about something bad happening if you didn't finish the pattern was definitely true, even if others didn't understand why?

I don't know if I really... I didn't think about it in terms of it being a definite fact, or whether the other guys understood it or not. I wasn't really focused on them at all. 

It was just... I just had that overwhelming feeling that I needed to finish it. I didn't really stop to debate if it was true or if my lieutenant got what I was doing. I just knew I had to do it right then, so I didn't really think about the rest of it.
Did you think that your belief about something bad happening if you didn't finish the pattern was realistic?

I don't think I ever really stopped to consider if it was realistic or not. Um... when you're in the middle of it, you just feel this intense pressure. It wasn't about logic or being realistic. I just... I just felt like I had to do it, so I did. I wasn't really analyzing it at the time.
Did you think that your belief about something bad happening if you didn't finish the pattern was something that other people would understand if they were in your shoes?

I didn't really think about whether anyone else would understand it. I mean, I wasn't putting myself in their shoes or thinking about what they would do. I was just focused on the bags and getting it done. I don't know if they would have felt the same way or not, honestly. I just wasn't thinking about them at all.
Did you think that your belief about something bad happening if you didn't finish the pattern was based on facts or evidence?

No, I didn't... I wasn't looking for proof or anything like that. Like I was saying before, I just had this intense feeling. I wasn't sitting there weighing evidence or trying to find facts to back it up. I just felt the pressure to finish the pattern, and that was it. Facts didn't really enter into it at all.
Did you think that your belief about something bad happening if you didn't finish the pattern was true, even if it didn't make sense to others?

Yeah, I... I thought it was true. Like I said, it wasn't about what made sense to anybody else. They actually sent me here because of it. At the station, I just kept moving the airway bags into this pattern... I just knew it was the right way. I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud while I did it. My lieutenant told me to stop and step away, but I wouldn't. I couldn't. It just felt like the whole ambulance bay would go bad, like something terrible would happen if I broke the sequence. So, yeah, to me it was completely true in that moment.
Did you think that your belief about something bad happening if you didn't finish the pattern was false, even for a moment?

No, I didn't. I... I never thought it was false. Like I just said, it felt completely real to me at the time. There wasn't any point where I stopped and doubted it, or thought it wasn't true. I was just completely focused on getting the bags in the right sequence so nothing bad would happen.
Did you think that your belief about something bad happening if you didn't finish the pattern was a thought that you couldn't control?

I wouldn't really say it was a thought I couldn't control. I mean... I wasn't trying to stop it or fight it off. It wasn't like some random thought popping into my head against my will. It was just the reality of the situation to me. I just knew I had to finish the sequence with the airway bags, so that's what I was doing. I didn't feel like I was losing control of my own thoughts, I was just doing what had to be done.
Did you think that your belief about something bad happening if you didn't finish the pattern was a fact, regardless of what others thought?

Yeah, definitely. It was just... a fact. Like I was saying before, it didn't really matter what the lieutenant or anybody else thought about it. I knew what was going to happen if I didn't finish arranging those bags. So to me, yes, it was an absolute fact.
Did you think that your belief about something bad happening if you didn't finish the pattern was something that you could be mistaken about?

No, I didn't think I could be mistaken. I... I was completely sure about it. Like I was just saying, it was a fact to me. There wasn't any doubt in my mind that I was right about what would happen if I didn't finish with the bags. So, no, I didn't think I was wrong.
Did you think that your belief about something bad happening if you didn't finish the pattern was something that could be proven or disproven?

I didn't really think about it like that. I mean... I wasn't looking for proof, you know? It wasn't a theory or something I needed to test. I just knew it was true. So... I guess I wasn't thinking about whether someone could prove it or disprove it. It was just what was happening.
